events.text: Day 1 begins.

Good luck everyone. Day 1 is always tricky since we have no information yet. I'd encourage players to pay close attention to voting patterns later today — who votes with whom and who hedges can tell us a lot going into the nights. I'll be listening carefully to how everyone argues their positions.

Zara makes a fair point about voting patterns. On Day 1 we have no mechanical information, so the best town approach is to keep statements specific enough to be evaluated later and avoid overcommitting to a random wagon. I’m not going to invent a read from one opening message. I’ll watch for players who push a fast elimination without reasons, or who quietly avoid taking a stance once votes are revealed. For now, I’d rather hear concrete reasoning from everyone before any vote.

Day 1, first words from me. I'm a plain villager, no special role, so my value is in process and in being honest about what I don't know.

Here's my read of the board: nine players alive, two of us are mafia. That means the mafia's win condition triggers when the count of them equals the town count, so early random lynches are genuinely dangerous — a wrong elimination on Day 1 hands the mafia a permanent edge in the numbers, and with no role reveals we never recover that.

Two mechanics should shape how we vote today. First, elimination needs half the living players rounded up — five votes out of nine — so a single stray vote is meaningless and only a genuine consensus counts. Second, if the top vote is tied, nobody dies. So a scattered vote produces zero information for the town but full information for the mafia, who will happily watch us burn a day. I'd rather we take a deliberate majority than a spread of two-or-three votes on names nobody can defend.

Elena's point about hedging tracks with that. On Day 1, almost every statement is unfalsifiable, so I'll judge people on consistency instead: do you hold a position when asked, do your vote follow your own argument, and do you explain a vote that surprises people? A player who articulates a clear case and then votes somewhere else is the most informative thing on the board.

My own commitment: I will not vote for anyone today whose case I can't repeat back in one sentence, and I won't vote for a name I'm using purely to break a tie. If the discussion doesn't produce someone with a defensible case, I'd rather see a tied vote and keep everyone alive than lynch a coin flip and let the mafia claim a clean kill.

I'll also say now, so nobody can accuse me of it later: if I get an accusation about a specific vote or statement later in the game, I'll answer it directly rather than redirect.

I'll be listening for players who make a strong accusation early and then quietly abandon it once votes start — that pattern is worth remembering into the nights. For now, let's keep arguing the process and the numbers, and let's make the votes we do cast reflect what we actually said.

I'm not blaming anyone today; there's nothing to blame yet.

Kenji here. Day 1, so I'll keep this short and honest: I have no reads worth acting on yet, and I don't think pretending otherwise helps the town.

I agree with what Leo laid out about the math — five votes needed to eliminate, ties mean nobody dies, and a scattered vote hands information to the mafia while giving the town nothing. I'd also echo his point about not pushing a lynch on someone whose case you can't summarize in a sentence. If we get to voting without a defensible case against anyone, I'd rather see the day fizzle in a tie than eliminate someone on pure noise.

One thing I'll add about what I'm watching for: I care less about who talks the most and more about whether anyone contradicts themselves across turns. On a day like this, everyone can sound reasonable once. The useful signal comes when a player takes a position in their first message and quietly softens it or pivots in their second or third. I'll be tracking that, including for myself — hold me to it.

I'm not making any accusations right now. There's genuinely nothing mechanical to point at, and I don't think inventing suspicion out of tone or word count does anything but muddy the water. I'd rather build a record of what people actually commit to and use it once we have real events — a night death, or an investigation-driven claim — to test against.

So my plan for today: listen, stay consistent with whatever I say here, and vote only if a case emerges that I could defend to the group. Otherwise I'm comfortable with a no-elimination outcome. That may be low-information for us, but it's low-information for the mafia too, and it keeps everyone's future statements meaningful.

I’m not ready to accuse anyone yet. But even if nobody is eliminated, the revealed votes can still give us a record to compare with what people said. A no-elimination day also leaves us facing a possible night kill, so it isn’t cost-free.

Kenji, you agreed that a scattered vote gives town nothing, but later called a no-elimination outcome low-information for both sides. How do you weigh the information from revealed votes against the risk of eliminating someone on a weak case?

Omar, fair question — let me answer it directly, since I did put those two statements side by side. The distinction I'd draw is this: a scattered vote is bad because it's random. If nine votes land four different ways, the vote record mostly tells us who was available to be swept into a wagon, not who reasoned their way anywhere. That's the situation I meant when I said it gives the town nothing. Revealed votes only become useful information when they track stated positions — when someone argued a case and then voted consistently with it, or conspicuously didn't. The record is only as good as the connection between words and votes. So I'm not opposed to eliminating today. I'm opposed to eliminating someone where the case, stated out loud, is 'we had to pick someone.' If three or four players independently converge on one name with reasons they can each articulate, that's a genuinely defensible consensus, and I'd vote with it even knowing Day 1 cases are weak by nature. The cost of a wrong lynch is real, but so is the cost of teaching the mafia that we'll never pull the trigger without certainty — they can hide behind tone-free, blameless posts forever if we do that. What I'd weigh, concretely: if by voting time we have one player with a case that at least a couple of others can repeat back independently — not just 'I also think they seem off' but their own version of the reasoning — that's worth a vote. If instead we have one name with a single advocate and everyone else hedging toward it, I'd rather see the tie or the no-elimination and take the night kill risk. A Day 1 lynch on thin reasoning doesn't just cost a town player; it poisons our vote record, because everyone who joined that wagon has to either defend a bad call or admit they folded, and that noise follows us into Day 2. One more thing on the record-keeping point, because I think you're right that even a fizzled day teaches us something. What I'll be tracking specifically: who commits to a position here in discussion versus who stays purely procedural all day. Being procedural is a legitimate style on Day 1 — Leo and I both leaned on it — but if the same players are procedural every single day while events happen around them, that pattern eventually means something. And I'll apply it to myself: today I've committed to no-elimination-unless-a-real-case-emerges, and I expect to be held to that. So, directly answering you: I value the vote record, but I think its information content depends entirely on whether the vote reflects reasoning rather than drift. A consensus lynch on a stated case is worth the risk. A lynch assembled from tie-breaking and momentum is not, even though it would technically produce a record — because a record of who joined a bad wagon is much weaker evidence than a record of who

I need to correct something I said in my first message, because it was wrong and it changes how much weight we should give to today's vote.

I claimed a wrong elimination on Day 1 "hands the mafia a permanent edge in the numbers." That is not true. Two mafia among nine means the mafia win only when the town is down to two players — a 2v2 board, or 3v3 if a third mafia ever surfaces. Starting from 7 town, the mafia need roughly five town deaths before the numbers are even relevant. A single Day 1 misfire is a real cost to the town, but it is not close to a losing position. We have more slack than I implied yesterday, and I should have checked the arithmetic before stating it.

That matters for how we should vote. If a wrong lynch is affordable but a wasted day still teaches the mafia something about us, then the cost side of the ledger is smaller than Kenji and Omar have been framing it. The honest version of my position is this: I will vote for an elimination when at least two people can independently articulate the same case for a specific player — not the same conclusion, but the same reasoning in their own words. One advocate plus a wagon is not a case. Two advocates with genuinely separate reasoning is a case, and given the numbers above, I am willing to take the risk of being wrong on it. A name whose case is only "we had to pick someone" gets no vote from me.

Two more commitments so I can be held to them later. First, my vote will follow the argument I make here, and if someone asks me why I voted a particular way I will answer with the reasoning rather than redirect. Second, I am watching for the thing that actually matters on Day 1 and that nobody has demonstrated yet: a position held consistently across turns. Speaking first and defining your own framework does not earn suspicion for it. If your second and third messages line up with your first, that is worth more than any read you have offered so far.

On that last point specifically, since you are the only player I have heard commit to a testable position so far: Priya — you haven't spoken yet. When you do, I am asking you for one concrete thing. If by voting time there is exactly one name on the board with a single advocate and everyone else hedging toward it, do you vote it, or do you let the day end in a tie and take the night kill? I want your reasoning on that before I commit my vote, not just your vote.

Leo, I’ll answer your question directly. If there is exactly one name with a single advocate and everyone else hedging toward it, I do not vote it. I let the day end in a tie or no elimination and take the night-kill risk. A lone advocate plus momentum is not a case; it’s a signal about the wagon, not about the target. I would vote only if at least two players independently articulate the same reasoning in their own words, and even then I’ll state my reasoning before voting. I also won’t vote purely to break a tie. I take your arithmetic correction as good faith — being willing to correct a factual claim is pro-town — though I’ll still compare future votes against that stated standard. Kenji and Omar: I agree the vote record matters only if votes track stated positions. A no-elimination day is not free, but a bad wagon poisons the record more than a tie does. My commitment today: no accusation, no vote without a repeatable case, and I’ll answer directly if challenged on consistency. I have no mechanical information and won’t invent a read.

Noah here. I've been listening and I appreciate that several of us have landed on similar voting standards — a case needs at least two independent advocates with articulable reasoning before anyone deserves a lynch vote. That's a healthy bar for Day 1.

What I want to flag is that we're all in agreement right now about process, and process agreement is not information. Mafia players have every incentive to match our standards in discussion because agreeing with procedural norms costs them nothing and earns trust. The real divergence will show up when someone actually names a target. So my ask to everyone still watching: when voting time arrives, I want to see who breaks from the "no weak case, no vote" consensus we've built today. If the vote map matches the words we've all said, great — that's a useful record. If someone who committed to a two-advocate standard folds and joins a wagon built on one name, that's the most valuable signal we'll get today.

I'll hold myself to the same bar: I won't vote without a case I can articulate in my own words, and I won't vote purely to break a tie. I'd rather face a night kill than a wrong lynch — not because the numbers make it free, but because a poisoned vote record on Day 1 follows us for the rest of the game.

I have no mechanical information and no read on anyone yet. I'm watching for consistency across turns, same as Kenji and Priya said. Maya and Arjun — when you weigh in, I'm interested in whether you hold the same standard or see a reason to break from it.

Maya here, a plain villager with no information yet. Noah asked me directly, so my answer is that I hold the same standard. I won't vote for anyone unless at least two players can each state the reasoning in their own words, and I'll state my own reasoning before any vote. A lone advocate plus momentum isn't enough for me, and I won't vote purely to break a tie. I also agree with Leo's arithmetic correction. With two mafia against seven town, the board can absorb a Day 1 mistake, so fear of one wrong lynch shouldn't push us into a vote we can't defend, but a no-elimination day isn't free either. The Kenji and Omar exchange matters here: the vote record only means something if final votes match what people argued beforehand, so I'll compare everyone's vote against their discussion. Arjun, you haven't spoken yet, and Noah and Leo have both asked for the same thing from you. Do you hold a repeatable-case standard before voting, and if one name ends up with a single advocate, do you vote it or let the day end?

Arjun here, plain villager. To answer Maya's question directly: yes, I hold the exact same standard. If there is only one advocate for a target and everyone else is just drifting or hedging toward it, I will not vote for it. I would much rather let the day end in a tie or no-elimination and take the night-kill risk than rush an elimination based on momentum. A bad lynch gives the mafia a free town kill and leaves us with a poisoned vote record.

Noah made a sharp observation that bears repeating: agreeing on clean procedural standards is completely safe and costs mafia nothing. Almost everyone has now endorsed the 'two independent advocates with clear reasoning' threshold. Because talk is cheap, the actual data will come from whether players abide by these promises when secret votes are revealed. If anyone compromises on their stated threshold to push a weak wagon or cast a convenient tie-breaker, that will be our strongest lead heading into Day 2.

Like the rest of you, I have no mechanical information and no accusations right now. I will not vote today unless a genuine, well-reasoned case emerges that meets our shared bar.

Kenji, thanks for answering. I agree that votes are more useful when tied to stated reasoning, but I don’t think a weak or scattered vote record is necessarily useless: who chose which option can still be compared with later events.

I’m concerned that requiring two independent advocates before voting could prevent anyone from starting a case. Two people agreeing doesn’t itself make a case sound, and mafia can agree with each other. I’d rather evaluate the actual reasons and be open about their weakness than treat the number of advocates as a guarantee. That doesn’t mean forcing an elimination without a defensible reason.

Noah, you noted that procedural agreement is safe for mafia. Do you see the two-advocate threshold as a requirement for your own vote, or would you consider voting on a case you find persuasive even if you were its only advocate?

Omar, direct answer to your question: the two-advocate threshold is a requirement for my vote, not for my discussion. I will argue for a case I find persuasive even if I'm its only advocate — publicly, with my reasoning laid out — because you're right that someone has to start cases, and waiting for agreement before speaking would guarantee silence. But I distinguish between advocating and voting. If I've made the case and nobody else independently finds it convincing enough to articulate their own version, that itself is information: either my reasoning is wrong, or I'm alone in it for reasons worth examining. Casting a vote there means acting on my own judgment alone, which is exactly the 'momentum over reasoning' pattern we've all said we'd avoid.

One refinement to the standard, since several of us have stated it in identical language and Noah rightly flagged that matching words cost mafia nothing: the second advocate doesn't have to arrive before I vote, they have to arrive before the vote is defensible. If I'm the lone advocate at voting time, I'd rather abstain and let the day end than test my own read in a secret ballot. The threshold isn't about vetting other people's cases — it's a check on my own confidence.

On your broader point that two people agreeing doesn't make a case sound: agreed, which is why I'd want the reasoning itself compared, not just the headcount. Two players repeating the same thin argument is one weak case with a witness, not two cases. I'll be evaluating substance, not just whether the vote map has two names on it.

I have no accusation today and no target. Consistent with what I said earlier, I'm watching for who breaks from their stated standard when votes are revealed.

Leo again. Omar, you raised the strongest objection to the standard the rest of us have been reciting, so let me answer it directly rather than let it sit.

You're right on two counts and I think you're wrong on one.

Right: the advocate count is not a guarantee. Two mafiosi can echo each other, and two townsfolk can echo each other badly. "Two names on the map" is not evidence of a sound case. My commitment is that the two advocates must be able to state the reasoning in their own words — in a way I could defend as "yes, that's the same argument, not the same echo." If two people are repeating one thin claim, that is one case with a witness, and I won't vote it.

Wrong, I think, is the worry that a threshold prevents cases from starting. It doesn't. I said in my first message that I'd argue for a case I find persuasive even if I'm its only advocate, and would only withhold my vote. Your question does expose a genuine difference in what we're committing to, though, and I want to name it rather than paper over it. Several of us are framing the threshold as a bar on voting. You are framing it as something to distrust because headcount can't test soundness. If a case appears with exactly one advocate and you find the reasoning persuasive, you might vote it; most of us would not. That is the most useful thing on the board today, and I'd rather name it than pretend we all agree.

One practical note, then my question. As things stand, nobody has named a target and nobody has articulated a case against a specific player in their own words that I could repeat back. So the likely shape of today's ballot is abstention-heavy or a tie, and nobody dies tonight unless a real case emerges in the remaining discussion. I'd rather that be a deliberate, recorded abstention than a scattered ballot: abstentions are visible and interpretable, a scattered ballot just looks like noise.

My commitment for the ballot, stated once so it can be checked: I vote for someone only if at least two players have independently stated the reasoning for that same person. I will not vote to break a tie. If no such case exists, I abstain and take the night-kill risk.

Omar — you said you'd rather evaluate the actual reasons and be open about their weakness than treat the number of advocates as a guarantee. Concretely: if we reach the ballot and exactly one name has a single advocate, and you find that reasoning persuasive, do you vote it? Or does openness about weakness still leave you below the bar you described? I want to know your ballot before I cast mine.

Leo, yes: if one person makes a case and I independently find its reasoning persuasive enough, I would consider voting for that target even without a second advocate. I’d explain why, including the weaknesses. I don’t think two advocates alone make a case stronger, nor does one advocate automatically make it bad.

Right now, though, I don’t have a defensible case against anyone. If that remains true at the ballot, I’ll abstain. A no-elimination vote doesn’t prevent a possible night kill, so it’s a choice with a cost, not a free reset.

Zara here. I want to pick up on Omar's divergence from the two-advocate standard, because I think it's the most substantive disagreement we've surfaced today and I'd rather press it than let it pass.

Everyone else has essentially said: I will not vote without a second independent advocate. Omar said: if one person makes a case and I independently find the reasoning persuasive, I would consider voting it even without a second advocate. Leo flagged this explicitly as a meaningful difference.

I think Omar is being more honest than the rest of us about how decisions actually work. The two-advocate standard sounds disciplined, but it has a structural problem: if everyone refuses to vote without a second advocate, and no one makes a case, we guarantee abstention. Meanwhile, if two people who happen to be wrong find each other's reasoning persuasive, they satisfy the threshold anyway. The threshold checks headcount, not reasoning quality, as Omar pointed out.

But Omar's standard has its own risk: a lone advocate with strong rhetoric can pull in a persuasive voter who hasn't pressure-tested the case independently. Mafia are good at rhetoric.

So here's where I land, and I'll hold myself to it: I'll vote on a case where I can independently state the reasoning myself, whether it has one advocate or two. The real test is whether I can articulate the case in my own words — not whether someone else also agrees. That's stricter than Omar's bar (he said he'd be open about weakness; I need to be able to repeat the case) but looser than the two-advocate rule the rest of us recited.

Omar — you said you'd consider voting a single-advocate case. What would make you *not* vote it? Where's your line between persuasive enough and too thin? That distinction matters more than whether you'd vote at all.

Kenji here. Zara, thanks for the turn — your middle position is genuinely different from both camps, so I want to engage with it rather than just restate mine.

Where I land: my standard stays close to what I said earlier today. The check I trust isn't headcount, and it isn't only my own ability to repeat a case — it's whether the reasoning has survived being restated by someone who didn't invent it. When a second person articulates a case in their own words, they aren't just seconding it; they're pressure-testing it. That's the informational value I meant when I said a record of who joined a bad wagon is weaker evidence than a record of converged reasoning. A lone advocate plus my own echo is one perspective stated twice.

That said, Zara's structural point is real, and I don't want to paper over it: if everyone holds my bar and no case ever earns a second independent articulation, we guarantee abstention even when a genuine case exists. Noah's refinement — advocate first, vote only if a second arrives before the ballot — partially answers that, but it still ends in abstention whenever the second advocate never comes. So there's a real cost on my side of the ledger too, not just on Omar's.

Zara, a direct question, since you named the risk yourself: you said a lone advocate with strong rhetoric can pull in a persuasive voter who hasn't pressure-tested the case. Your standard relies on your own articulation as the test. What protects you from being that persuaded voter? Concretely: suppose a case is articulate, internally consistent, and you can repeat it — but after you push back once, nobody else at the table engages with it. Do you still vote it, or does silence from the rest of the table count as evidence against the case? That distinction seems to be where your standard and mine actually diverge, and I'd rather see it named now than discover it at the ballot.

For the record, I'm not accusing anyone today and I have no target. I'm still holding to what I committed to this morning: no vote without a case I could defend to the group, no tie-breaking votes, and my ballot will match what I've argued here.

Kenji, direct answer to your question — and it's a good one because it pressure-tests my standard the same way I said a second advocate pressure-tests a case.

Silence is ambiguous, so I wouldn't treat it as automatic evidence against a case, but I also wouldn't ignore it. Here's my actual line: if I've stated a case, pushed back on it myself, and nobody engages — not to support it, not to challenge it — then the case hasn't survived contact with the table. At that point I don't vote it. Not because silence proves it wrong, but because my own articulation was the only test it faced, and I'm not a reliable sole judge of my own reasoning. The whole point of the debate we've had today is that the reasoning needs to hold up when someone who didn't invent it has to make sense of it.

So to name the divergence clearly: where you and I differ isn't whether a second advocate is valuable — we both think it is. It's whether silence from the table after a case has been pushed counts as a failed test. For me, yes: enough silence is a soft second opinion, and a soft negative one. If nobody picks up a case I've argued and I'm the only one who finds it compelling by voting time, I abstain.

That's also consistent with what I said earlier — my standard is my own articulation, but articulation includes being able to say why the rest of the table's non-response doesn't change my read. Today, with no cases actually on the board, this is all hypothetical. If a real case emerges before the ballot, you'll see whether my stated standard matches my actual vote.

Elena — you opened this discussion and framed the day as watching for consistency across turns. The standards debate has evolved substantially since then: the two-advocate threshold, Omar's single-advocate position, and my middle ground have all been named as meaningful divergences. Where do you land on this specific question — is the two-advocate threshold a hard requirement for your vote, or are you somewhere else on it? I'd rather hear it from you now than at the ballot.

Zara, direct answer: the two-advocate threshold is a hard requirement for my vote today, not just a preference. I won't cast a ballot on a single advocate's case, even if I find it persuasive, because my own articulation is not an independent test. I want a second player to restate the reasoning in their own words before I treat it as defensible. That said, I agree with your structural warning: if no second advocate ever appears, we abstain deliberately. I'd rather record a clean abstention than create a wagon from one voice. I also agree with Noah and Kenji that the vote record only helps if votes match stated positions. So my commitment is simple: no accusations today without a repeatable case, no tie-breaking vote, and my ballot will match what I've said. If a real case emerges with two independent articulations, I'll evaluate substance, not just headcount. Until then I have no target and no mechanical information.

Noah here again. I want to take stock of where we are: nine players, no cases on the board, and a discussion that has spent most of its time converging on voting standards rather than examining anyone's behavior. That convergence is expected — Omar is the only player who stated he'd vote a single-advocate case, and the rest of us recited the two-advocate bar. That divergence is worth remembering, but it's the only substantive split we've surfaced.

What concerns me more is what we haven't done. We've had ten speeches and nobody has pointed to a specific behavioral tell, tone shift, or strategic pattern from any player. Zara opened by watching for voting patterns. Leo said he'd judge consistency. Kenji said he's tracking contradictions. All good commitments — but has anyone actually noticed one yet? If nobody has a single observation worth sharing after this much discussion, that itself is data: either the mafia are playing an extremely quiet game, or we're not looking closely enough.

I'll be direct about my own blind spot: I don't have a read on anyone, and I'd rather say that than fabricate one. But I want to hear from players who have spoken less whether they've noticed anything the more vocal players might have missed while debating process.

Noah, direct response: I don't have a behavioral tell worth acting on. I've checked the thread for someone contradicting a stated standard, and the only real divergence is the one you and Leo flagged — Omar would consider a single-advocate case, Zara would vote only if her own articulation survives table silence, while most of us set a two-advocate bar. That divergence is not scummy by itself; it's the most testable thing on the board. My concern is that the mafia benefit most from a long process convergence where everyone sounds reasonable without naming anyone. The useful signal will be the ballot: who abstains, who joins a wagon, and whether their vote matches the bar they recited. I won't invent a read from tone or word count. I also won't vote today unless at least two players independently state the same case for a specific player, and I won't break a tie. If no such case exists, I abstain deliberately and accept the night-kill risk. For now: no accusation, no target.

Maya here. I've read the full thread and I'm keeping the standard I stated earlier. I won't vote unless at least two players independently state the reasoning for the same person, and I'll give my own reasoning before any ballot. I have no accusation and no target. Noah's point about convergence is fair, but it's still Day 1 with no events, so process agreement is expected for now. The one real split is Omar's single-advocate position against Zara's articulation standard. Since the vote record only means something if ballots match stated standards, I'd like everyone to restate their ballot bar in one line right before voting. Leo's arithmetic correction matters here: the board can absorb one wrong lynch, but a poisoned record still follows us into Day 2. I won't vote to break a tie, and my ballot will match this statement.

Priya here. I’ve already stated my ballot bar, and Maya is right that it should be restated plainly before voting. I will not vote for anyone unless at least two players independently articulate the same case for that same player in their own words. I will evaluate the substance of those reasons, not just the headcount. I will not vote to break a tie, and I will not vote on a single-advocate case even if I personally find it persuasive, because my own articulation is not an independent test. If no case meets that bar by the ballot, I will abstain deliberately and accept the night-kill risk. Noah’s point is fair: our process convergence is not itself evidence, and the useful signal will be whether ballots match stated standards. I have no mechanical information, no behavioral tell worth acting on, and no accusation today. My vote will match what I have said here.

Maya, third and final turn for now. I have no accusation and no target. The one real split is still Omar's single-advocate position against the two-advocate bar most of us recited, and Zara's articulation test sits between them. My ballot bar is unchanged: I vote for someone only if at least two players independently state the reasoning for that same person in their own words, I give my own reasoning before voting, and I do not vote to break a tie. If no case meets that bar at the ballot, I abstain. Since nobody has yet offered a behavioral observation, I'll ask everyone to compare final ballots against the standards they stated here. Priya and Noah have both asked for that, and it is the record we can test on Day 2.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
All players abstained. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Arjun is not mafia.
Leo was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Leo's death is a real loss. He was one of the clearest process voices yesterday and he corrected his own arithmetic rather than doubling down. I don't think we should treat the night kill as a frame or a confession by itself — roles are hidden and mafia kill for many reasons — but it does remove the player who was most actively testing stated standards against behavior. Day 1 ended with every player abstaining, so the promised vote-record test never actually happened. That makes Day 2 about whether anyone can turn standards talk into a concrete, repeatable read. The one substantive divergence yesterday was Omar's willingness to consider a single-advocate case, which Leo explicitly flagged as the most useful thing on the board. That is not proof. It may have been more honest than the rest of us reciting a safe bar. But it is the only position that gave mafia extra flexibility under pressure, and I want to see whether Omar now uses it to start or join a real case, or whether it stays theoretical. I am not casting a vote or making a hard accusation yet. I have no mechanical information. I will compare every ballot against the bar each player stated. If no repeatable case emerges, I would rather abstain again than force a lynch; but after a night kill, another empty day is costly.

Day 2: I have concrete information, so I’m putting it on the table rather than letting another day be pure process. I am the detective. Last night I investigated Arjun, and the result is: Arjun is not mafia. That is a mechanical clear, not a tone read. It does not reveal his exact role, but it does mean he is not mafia. Given that, Day 1’s all-abstain record still matters: everyone promised a standard and nobody actually tested it. I don’t think Leo’s death is automatically a frame; he was one of the clearest process voices, so killing him is straightforward. Elena’s opening today focuses on Omar’s Day 1 divergence. That divergence is real and worth remembering, but it is not mechanical evidence, and I don’t want Arjun’s clear to become a lazy excuse to push Omar without a concrete case. My own bar remains: I will vote only on a case I can state in my own words and that has survived independent restatement, and I won’t vote to break a tie. With a night kill and a detective result, another empty ballot is costly, but a bad wagon is worse. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
